3 JUDGMENT :
[PER : SHYAM C. CHANDAK, J.] :-

1 ) Present Appeal filed under Section 11 of The Maharashtra P.H. Jayani 72 APEAL488.2023 FINAL.doc Protection of Interest of Depositors (In Financial Establishments) Act, 1999 (for short 'MPID Act') challenges the Order dated 08 th February 2023, passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Pune thereby rejecting Criminal Misc. Application No.23 of 2022 (for short 'the Application') filed under Section 156 (3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (for short ' Cr.P.C.') seeking direction to Shivaji Nagar/any other Police Station, Pune to register F.I.R. and set out investigation for the offences punishable under Sections 406, 409, 420 read with 120-B and Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and Sections 3 and 4 of the MPID Act,
against Respondent Nos.2 to 7, who were arraigned as accused Nos.1 to 6 in the said Application.
1.1) Hereinafter, the parties are being referred to by their original status in the Application i.e.,
Appellants as 'Complainants' and Respondent Nos.2 to 6 as 'Accused'.
2) Heard Mr. Nashikkar, Advocate for the Appellants, Mr. Rajiv Chavan, learned Senior Advocate for the accused and Mrs. Takalkar, learned APP for the State.

3) The facts giving rise to this Appeal are as under :-
3.1) The Complainants are engaged in the business of sale and sup ply of timber,
plywood and doors in the name and styled as M/s. Variety Plywood and M/s. Namo Sales.
Accused nos.1 and 2 have been doing the business of development of Real Estate, construction and allied activities.

The accused nos.3 to 6 are partners of accused no.1 and accused nos.3 and P.H. Jayani 72 APEAL488.2023 FINAL.doc 4 are partners of accused no.2.
3.2)
That, the accused persons informed the Complainants that, they are in constant requirement of funds for their business.

Therefore, they have floated a scheme namely 'Short Term Advance Interest Deposit Scheme', wherein the accused persons will accept deposits for a short period of three months and pay interest @ 1.5% per month i.e., 18% per annum in advance and return the principal amount after expiry of three months.

Then, the accused persons requested the Complainant Nos.1 to 3 to advance an amount for an initial period of three months starting from the date of deposit and promised to pay the interest in advance.
Accordingly, the Complainant Nos.1 to 3 deposited Rs.33,00,000/- in the said scheme in favour of accused no.2.

sentences.text: Thereafter, despite repeated requests by Complainant Nos.1 to 3, the accused persons did not return the balance principal amount of Rs.28,50,000/- along with the interest of Rs.13,05,495/-.
However, the Complainant Nos.1 to 3 repeatedly followed up with the accused.
Finally, the accused persons issued 08 cheques for the total amount of Rs.41,05,495/-, drawn on different bankers and promised the Complainant Nos.1 to 3 that, the said cheques would be honoured.
However, the said cheques dishonoured when presented for encashment.

3.6) Thus, the accused persons deceived the Complainant Nos.1 to 3 and dishonestly induced them to invest/deposit Rs.33,00,000/- in the said scheme of the accused but without any intention to repay the same with the accrued interest therein.
3.7) It is alleged that, in the meantime, after gaining the confidence of the Complainants in respect of the said investment of Rs.33,00,000/-, the accused persons told the Complainant Nos.3 to 8

that,
they have floated a real estate scheme i.e., 'Buy Back Scheme' in respect of a land bearing Gat P.H.
Jayani 72 APEAL488.2023 FINAL.doc No.372, Amberwadi, Khandala, Satara.
That, money deposited in the said scheme will be multiplied into eight times and it will be returned after two years.
In the alternative, the Complainants will have an option to retain certain plots in the said land, instead of taking back the deposited money, but upon payment of certain amount.
Relying upon the said representations and assurances by the accused persons, which evidently were malicious, the Complainant nos.3 to 8 invested Rs.8,36,000/-.

The accused persons assured that,
against the said investment, they would pay Rs.62,72,685/- inclusive of the principal amount, upon expiration of 24 months in a phased manner in the form of postdated cheques.

Alternatively, the Complainant Nos.3 to 8 will have an option of retaining plot nos.55, 56, 61 and 101 total admeasuring about 7197 sq. ft. i.e., 673.24 sq. mts., which were offered as security, upon payment of Rs.7,14,334/-, at the time of handing over of possession of the said plots.
Accordingly, the Complainant Nos.3 to 8 and accused persons entered into the Agreements (MoUs) dated 20.08.2017 and 25.08.2017.

At the time of execution of the MoU, the accused persons drew several cheques in favour of the Complainants for a total amount of Rs.62,72,685/- with a promise that, the said cheques would be honoured.
3.8) It is alleged that, after expiry of the agreed two years period, the Complainant Nos.3 to 8 requested the accused persons to pay the agreed amount of Rs.62,72,685/-.
Meanwhile, Complainant No.4 deposited one of the cheques drawn in his favour.
However, the said cheque was P.H. Jayani 72 APEAL488.2023 FINAL.doc dishonoured.
Therefore, the Complainant Nos.3 to 8 requested the accused persons to honour the cheques.
However, the accused persons sought time giving the reason of financial constraints.
Thereafter, on numerous occasions the Complainants followed up with the accused and demanded the agreed amount, however in vain.
The demand notice dated 13 th December, 2021 issued to the accused persons yielded no results.

Thus,
the accused persons deceived the Complainant Nos.3 to 8 and dishonestly, induced them to deposit Rs.8,36,000/- in the ' Buy Back Scheme' but without any intention to pay the principal amount with agreed benefits thereto.
It is stated that, the accused persons siphoned the invested amount to shell entities/sister companies.
The total defrauded amount was Rs.36,86,000/-.
Therefore, the accused persons committed the offences punishable under Sections 420, 406, 409 read with Sections 120-B and 34 of I.P.C. and Sections 3 and 4 of the MPID Act.

Consequently, the Complainants sent their written complaint dated 25 th December, 2021 to the Shivajinagar Police Station, Swargate Police Station, Marketyard Police Station and various higher police authorities, Pune.

sentences.text: After considering the complaint in the light of the submissions made by Advocate for the Complainants, the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Pune held that, after filing of the Application under Section 156(3) P.H. Jayani 72 APEAL488.2023 FINAL.doc of Cr.P.C., the accused persons invoked arbitration proceedings against Complainants and the Complainants participated in the Arbitration proceedings.
The Arbitrator passed an award and directed the accused to pay certain amounts to the Complainants.
There was MoU in respect of the subject monetary transactions.
As such, the Complainants knew that, the aforesaid monetary transactions between the parties were of civil nature.
Even though the accused persons avoided to repay the amounts, the Complainants have not taken prompt legal steps.
Therefore, the Complainants cannot claim that, the accused persons committed the said offences.
Lastly, the learned Judge held that, the Complainants were trying to give a color of crime to the civil transactions.
This led the learned Judge to dismiss the Application.
Hence, the present Appeal.
4) Mr. Nashikar, Advocate for the Complainants submitted that, the investment schemes floated by the accused were completely nonviable in the financial world.
However, giving allurement of very high returns, the accused persons trapped the Complainants to enter into those schemes by investing their monies under oral agreement and MoU.
When the accused persons could not repay the subject amounts and the benefit accrued thereon, they renewed the investments from time to time accepting that liability under negotiable instruments etc.

Thus, the accused persons deceived the Complainants and dishonestly induced them to invest their monies in the said schemes but without any intention to return the P.H. Jayani 72 APEAL488.2023 FINAL.doc principal amount along with the agreed benefit i.e., compensation/interest accrued thereon.

Taking the entire facts and circumstances of the case together, it is evident that, the amount invested by the Complainants is a 'Deposit' as defined in Section 2(c) of the MPID Act and the accused persons are falling in the definition of 'Financial Establishments' as defined under Section 2(d) of the MPID Act.

Therefore,
the said act of the accused is an offence under Sections 420, 406, 409 read with Section 120-B and 34 of I.P.C. and Sections 3 and 4 of the MPID Act.
However, the learned Judge completely ignored the above and erroneously held that, the transaction in question is of civil nature.
Therefore, the impugned Order is not sustainable in law and is liable to be quashed.

To buttress his submissions,
the learned Advocate placed his reliance on following decisions.
We have carefully considered the same.

i) State of Maharashtra vs. 63 Moons Technologies, (2024) SCC OnLine SC 223,
ii) Rajiv Ramanlal Shah vs. Senior Inspector of Police, Criminal Writ Petition No.1224 of 2001 dtd.
24/01/2002'

sentences.text: Per contra, Mr. Rajiv Chavan, learned Senior Advocate for the accused submitted that, the monetary transactions between Complainants and the accused persons were of purely civil nature.

Even though, the Complainants alleged that, after expiry of two years period they cancelled the MoU and requested for the compensation/interest amount, no notice to that effect was issued by the Complainants to the accused persons.
The Complainants have not obtained the option of purchasing the proposed plots by paying the balance consideration.
Considering these facts and the delay in filing the Application, the learned Additional Judge has rightly held that, this is purely a case of civil nature.
Hence, the rejection of the Application cannot be questioned by way of this Appeal.

5.1)
Learned APP submitted that, considering the facts and circumstances of the case necessary Orders in the interest of justice may be passed.

6) From the perusal of Application under Section 156(3) of Cr.PC., it is evident that, the initial monetary transactions between the Complainant Nos.1 to 3 and the accused persons were purely of civil nature, as the amounts paid by the Complainant Nos.1 to 3 were towards the need of the funds,
expressed by the accused persons.
Secondly, the benefit which the Complainant Nos.1 to 3 agreed to receive against that monies from the accused persons was in the form of interest.
The Complainant Nos.1 to 3 have admitted the said fact of receiving the interest P.H. Jayani 72 APEAL488.2023 FINAL.doc from time to time.

The promissory notes/receipts produced on record also show that,
only interest was agreed to be paid to the said Complainants against their monies paid to the accused persons as loan.
The said initial investments by Complainant Nos.1 to 3 were made in October 2013, March 2015 and December 2014.
However prompt steps were not taken by them to recover the said amounts.
On the contrary, as alleged, they agreed to continue the investment by accepting the interest.
The Complainant Nos.1 to 3 have not satisfactorily explained as to why they have not taken prompt legal steps to recover their monies and lodged police report if they were cheated.
No payment receipts were executed containing the nature of transaction when the monies were originally paid by Appellant Nos.1 to 3.
There is considerable time gap between giving the loan amounts and the said receipts.
The receipts produced do not mention that, the said amounts were investment or deposit.

6.1) Thus, it is apparent that, the transactions between the Complainant Nos.1 to 3 and the accused persons were of money lending and not of investment or deposit under the alleged scheme floated by the accused persons.
6.2) From the MoU it is evident that, the prospective returns were highly excessive.
In the said Application itself the Complainant Nos.3 to 8 have stated that, the representations about the huge returns made by the accused persons were malicious.

Thus, since inception the Complainants P.H.
Jayani 72 APEAL488.2023 FINAL.doc knew the aforesaid facts, however, they entered into the monetary transactions including the MoU.
Therefore, it cannot be said that, the accused persons deceived the Complainants and dishonestly induced them to enter into the said MoU.

sentences.text: As regards the monetary transactions with Appellant Nos. 3 to 8, even though the initial monies of Appellant Nos.1 to 3 were not returned, the Appellant Nos.3 to 8 entered into the transaction with accused persons.

This fact indicates that, like Appellant Nos.1 to 3, these Appellants also entered into the said transaction on their own, willingly and after understanding its minute details only to earn an exorbitant interest and knowingly taking risk of their monies.
In view thereof, the learned Additional Sessions Judge has rightly held that, the transactions between the parties were of civil nature.

6.4) Even though the investments in the alleged schemes were of different period, all the transactions have been clubbed together to show that, the cause of action for the same is common and just to create a picture of fraud of huge amount.
Thus, the said Application under Section 156 (3) of Cr.P.C. was nothing but a result of an improper legal advice to the Appellants.

7) In so far as the reported cases cited by the learned Advocate for the Complainants is concerned,
the facts of the said cases and the case in hand are distinct and therefore those are of no help to him.
P.H. Jayani 72 APEAL488.2023 F  8)
In view of the above discussion, we find no illegal impugned Order.
As a result, the Appeal is liable to be dismissed and is accordingly dismissed.

opennyai_summary.facts:
That, the accused persons informed the Complainants that, they are in constant requirement of funds for their business.
Therefore, they have floated a scheme namely 'Short Term Advance Interest Deposit Scheme', wherein the accused persons will accept deposits for a short period of three months and pay interest @ 1.5% per month i.e., 18% per annum in advance and return the principal amount after expiry of three months.
Therefore, the accused persons committed the offences punishable under Sections 420, 406, 409 read with Sections 120-B and 34 of I.P.C. and Sections 3 and 4 of the MPID Act.
This led to filing of the Application u/Sec.156 (3) of Cr.P.C.

opennyai_summary.arguments:
However, giving allurement of very high returns, the accused persons trapped the Complainants to enter into those schemes by investing their monies under oral agreement and MoU.
When the accused persons could not repay the subject amounts and the benefit accrued thereon, they renewed the investments from time to time accepting that liability under negotiable instruments etc.
Thus, the accused persons deceived the Complainants and dishonestly induced them to invest their monies in the said schemes but without any intention to return the P.H. Jayani 72 APEAL488.2023 FINAL.doc principal amount along with the agreed benefit i.e., compensation/interest accrued thereon.
Taking the entire facts and circumstances of the case together, it is evident that, the amount invested by the Complainants is a 'Deposit' as defined in Section 2(c) of the MPID Act and the accused persons are falling in the definition of 'Financial Establishments' as defined under Section 2(d) of the MPID Act.
Therefore,
the said act of the accused is an offence under Sections 420, 406, 409 read with Section 120-B and 34 of I.P.C. and Sections 3 and 4 of the MPID Act.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
6) From the perusal of Application under Section 156(3) of Cr.PC., it is evident that, the initial monetary transactions between the Complainant Nos.1 to 3 and the accused persons were purely of civil nature, as the amounts paid by the Complainant Nos.1 to 3 were towards the need of the funds,
expressed by the accused persons.
Secondly, the benefit which the Complainant Nos.1 to 3 agreed to receive against that monies from the accused persons was in the form of interest.
The Complainant Nos.1 to 3 have not satisfactorily explained as to why they have not taken prompt legal steps to recover their monies and lodged police report if they were cheated.
6.1) Thus, it is apparent that, the transactions between the Complainant Nos.1 to 3 and the accused persons were of money lending and not of investment or deposit under the alleged scheme floated by the accused persons.
As regards the monetary transactions with Appellant Nos. 3 to 8, even though the initial monies of Appellant Nos.1 to 3 were not returned, the Appellant Nos.3 to 8 entered into the transaction with accused persons.
This fact indicates that, like Appellant Nos.1 to 3, these Appellants also entered into the said transaction on their own, willingly and after understanding its minute details only to earn an exorbitant interest and knowingly taking risk of their monies.
In view thereof, the learned Additional Sessions Judge has rightly held that, the transactions between the parties were of civil nature.
6.4) Even though the investments in the alleged schemes were of different period, all the transactions have been clubbed together to show that, the cause of action for the same is common and just to create a picture of fraud of huge amount.
Thus, the said Application under Section 156 (3) of Cr.P.C. was nothing but a result of an improper legal advice to the Appellants.
7) In so far as the reported cases cited by the learned Advocate for the Complainants is concerned,
the facts of the said cases and the case in hand are distinct and therefore those are of no help to him.
